steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the lead section of an encyclopedia article on Agent Communication Language (ACL): what it is, the older protocols, and the newer generative-AI-based protocols, contrasting the two approaches.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Definition of ACL
- Earlier protocols (FIPA-ACL, KQML)
- Shift to generative AI agents; NLIP and its standardization
- Two categories of protocols
- Ontology based protocols
- Generative AI based protocols
- NLIP security and maintenance

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Definition: computer communication protocols for AI agents to communicate with each other
- Earlier protocols, proposed in 2007
  - FIPA-ACL (Foundation for Intelligent Physical Agents, standardization consortium)
  - KQML (Knowledge Query and Manipulation Language)
- Shift after generative AI surge (Transformers, Large language models)
  - "agent" no longer physical agents -> software systems built on Agentic AI principles
  - new protocol: Natural Language Interaction Protocol (NLIP)
  - application-level; between AI agents or human and AI agent
  - Ecma International (standards body, info and communication industry): 10 December 2025, five new standards + one technical report defining NLIP
- Two categories: ontology based vs. generative AI based
- Ontology based
  - common ontology between agents
  - ontology = part of agent's knowledge base: what kind of things it can deal with, how related
  - examples: FIPA-ACL, KQML
  - speech act theory: Searle, 1960s; enhanced by Winograd and Flores, 1970s
  - performatives aka Communicative Acts + meaning (e.g. ask-one)
  - content of performative not standardized, varies by system
  - FIPA-ACL implementation support: FIPA-OS, Jade
- Generative AI based (e.g. NLIP)
  - no shared ontology needed
  - generative AI models translate text, images, videos, other modalities into local ontology
  - hot-extensibility: same protocol, multiple communication needs
  - simpler version control: agents can use different versions of shared ontology
- NLIP designed with security in mind; maintained by Ecma Technical Community 56

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Agent Communication Language (ACL) is made up of computer communication protocols meant for AI agents to talk to each other.

In 2007 several protocols of this kind were proposed, including:

FIPA-ACL (from the Foundation for Intelligent Physical Agents, which is a standardization consortium)

KQML (Knowledge Query and Manipulation Language)

After the surge in generative AI using Transformers and Large language models, the meaning of agent changed and moved away from physical agents, so now it means software systems built on the principles of Agentic AI. One new protocol in this area is the Natural Language Interaction Protocol (NLIP). NLIP is an application-level communication protocol between AI Agents, or between a human and an AI agent. On 10 December 2025 Ecma International, a standards body that develops and publishes international standards for the information and communication industry, published five new standards and one technical report that define NLIP.

So agent communication protocols can be divided into two categories: ontology based agent communication protocols and generative AI based agent communication protocols.

- Ontology based protocols
  - common ontology shared between agents
  - ontology: part of agent's knowledge base describing what things it can deal with and how they relate
  - FIPA-ACL and KQML are examples
  - rely on speech act theory (Searle, 1960s; enhanced by Winograd and Flores, 1970s)
  - set of performatives (Communicative Acts) and meaning, e.g. ask-one
  - performative content not standardized, varies between systems
  - FIPA-ACL implemented in FIPA-OS and Jade
- Generative AI based protocols like NLIP
  - no shared ontology; generative AI models translate natural language text, images, videos etc. into local ontology
  - hot-extensibility, simpler version control (different agents, different versions of shared ontology)
- NLIP: designed with security in mind; developed and maintained by Ecma Technical Community 56

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Agent Communication Language (ACL) is made up of computer communication protocols meant for AI agents to talk to each other.

In 2007 several protocols of this kind were proposed, including:

FIPA-ACL (from the Foundation for Intelligent Physical Agents, which is a standardization consortium)

KQML (Knowledge Query and Manipulation Language)

After the surge in generative AI using Transformers and Large language models, the meaning of agent changed and moved away from physical agents, so now it means software systems built on the principles of Agentic AI. One new protocol in this area is the Natural Language Interaction Protocol (NLIP). NLIP is an application-level communication protocol between AI Agents, or between a human and an AI agent. On 10 December 2025 Ecma International, a standards body that develops and publishes international standards for the information and communication industry, published five new standards and one technical report that define NLIP.

So agent communication protocols can be divided into two categories: ontology based agent communication protocols and generative AI based agent communication protocols.

Ontology based protocols use a common ontology that is shared between the agents. An ontology is the part of an agent's knowledge base that describes what kinds of things the agent can deal with and how they relate to each other. Examples of these protocols are FIPA-ACL and KQML. They rely on speech act theory, which was developed by Searle in the 1960s and enhanced by Winograd and Flores in the 1970s. They define a set of performatives, also called Communicative Acts, and what they mean (e.g. ask-one). The content of the performative is not standardized and varies from system to system. Implementation support of FIPA-ACL is included in FIPA-OS and Jade.

Generative AI based protocols like NLIP do not need a shared ontology between the agents that are communicating. Instead they use generative AI models to translate natural language text, images, videos or other kinds of data into a local ontology. This gives hot-extensibility, where the same protocol can be used for many communication needs, and it makes version control simpler since different agents can use different versions of a shared ontology.

NLIP was designed with security in mind. The NLIP specification and standards are developed and maintained by Ecma Technical Community 56.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Agent Communication Language (ACL) consists of computer communication protocols that are intended for AI agents to communicate with each other.

In 2007, protocols of this nature were proposed which include:

FIPA-ACL[1] (by the Foundation for Intelligent Physical Agents, a standardization consortium)

KQML[2] (Knowledge Query and Manipulation Language)

After the surge in generative AI with the use of Transformers and Large language models, the definition of agent has shifted away from physical agents to mean software systems built using the principles of Agentic AI. A new protocol that has emerged in this area is the Natural Language Interaction Protocol (NLIP).[3] NLIP is an application-level communication protocol defined between AI Agents or between a human and an AI agent. Ecma International, a standards body which develops and publishes international standards for the information and communication industry, published on 10 December 2025 five new standards and one technical report defining the Natural Language Interaction Protocol (NLIP).[4]

As a result, agent communication protocols can be divided into two categories: ontology based agent communication protocols and generative AI based agent communication protocols.

Ontology based agent communication protocols use a common ontology between agents. An ontology is a part of the agent's knowledge base that describes what kind of things an agent can deal with and how they are related to each other. FIPA-ACL and KQML are examples of such protocols. These protocols rely on speech act theory developed by Searle in the 1960s[5] and enhanced by Winograd and Flores in the 1970s. They define a set of performatives, also called Communicative Acts, and their meaning (e.g. ask-one). The content of the performative is not standardized, but varies from system to system. Implementation support of FIPA-ACL is included in FIPA-OS[6,7] and Jade.[8]

Generative AI based agent communication protocols such as NLIP[9] do not require a shared ontology among communicating agents. Instead, they use generative AI models to translate natural language text, images, videos or other modalities of data into a local ontology. This provides for hot-extensibility, where the same protocol can be used for multiple communication needs, and simplifies version control since different agents can use different versions of a shared ontology.

NLIP has been designed with security considerations in mind.[10,11,12] The specification and standards that make up NLIP are developed and maintained by Ecma Technical Community 56.[13]
